meaning: anyhow, in any case, at any rate
headline: Dōse is どう (dō, “how”) plus せ, a clipping of せよ (seyo), the imperative of する (suru).

sources.quote: Compound of どう (dō, “how”) + せ (se, clipping of せよ (seyo), the imperative form of する (suru, “do”)).

headline: Ogamu is from older 拝む (orogamu), shifting from wogamu.

sources.quote: /wogamu/ > /ogamu/. From older 拝(おろが)む (orogamu).

headline: Hitsujuhin is 必需 (hitsuju, “need, requirement, essentialness”) plus 品 (-hin, “item, good”).

sources.quote: Compound of 必需(ひつじゅ) (hitsuju, “need, requirement, essentialness, indispensability”) + 品(ひん) (-hin, “item, good”). Compare the formation of Chinese 必需品 (bìxūpǐn).

headline: Shaburu is first attested in 1778.

sources.quote: First attested in 1778.

headline: Hikage is 日 (hi, “sun”) plus 陰 (kage, “shade”).

sources.quote: 日(ひ) (hi, “sun”) + 陰(かげ) (kage, “shade”)

headline: Kangae is the continuative stem of 考える (kangaeru, “to think”).

sources.quote: 連(れん)用(よう)形(けい) (ren'yōkei, “stem or continuative form”) of the verb 考(かんが)える (kangaeru, “to think”).

meaning: to talk, to chat, to chatter (same as 話す (はなす))
headline: Shaberu has no known origin, but is listed in the Nippo Jisho of 1603, with an earliest appearance possibly in the early 1300s.

sources.quote: Unknown.
Possible analyses include:
* Related to しゃぶしゃぶ (shabushabu), itself apparently an onomatopoeia.
* Derived as intensifying prefix しゃ (sha) attaching to a root form related to べりべり (beriberi, “talkatively; a talkative person”), べらべら (berabera, “bubblingly; talkatively”), べろ (bero, “tongue”).
Listed in the Nippo Jisho of 1603. Earliest appearance may be in the early 1300s during the Kamakura period.

headline: Kozeni is 小 (ko-, “little”) plus 銭 (zeni, “coins; money”).

sources.quote: 小(こ) (ko-, “little”) + 銭(ぜに) (zeni, “coins; money”)

headline: Arayuru is a fossilized passive of ar-, “to be, to exist”, one of the few expressions that kept the old passive marker.

sources.quote: From Old Japanese arayuru, the attributive form of the passive form of ar- “to be, to exist”. Note that the passive marker -(a)ye- (attributive form -(a)yuru) ceased to be used in Early Middle Japanese except in fossilized expressions such as あらゆる (arayuru) and いはゆる (ifayuru) and in kanbun.

headline: Hantai is from Sinitic 反對.

sources.quote: From Sinitic 反對.

headline: Horu, “to carve”, is a doublet of 掘る (horu, “to dig”), and went poru > ɸoru > horu.

sources.quote: poru > ɸoru > horu.
Doublet of 掘(ほ)る (horu, “to dig”).

headline: Kutōten is 句読 (kutō) plus 点 (ten).

sources.quote: From 句読(くとう) (kutō) + 点(てん) (ten).

headline: Sō ieba is そう (sō, “like that, so”) plus 言えば (ieba), literally “speaking of that....”.

sources.quote: From そう (sō, “like that, so”) + 言(い)えば (ieba, conditional form of 言(い)う (iu, “to say”)). Literally, “speaking of that....”

headline: Shokugyō is, by surface analysis, 職 (shoku) plus 業 (-gyō).

sources.quote: By surface analysis, 職(しょく) (shoku) + 業(ぎょう) (-gyō).

sources.quote: 御(お) (o-, honorific prefix) + 洒(しゃ)落(れ) (share)

headline: Min'yō is a calque of German Volkslied.

sources.quote: Calque of German Volkslied.

headline: Ossharu is an alteration of おおせある (ōse aru).

sources.quote: Alteration of おおせある (ōse aru).

headline: Kona appears to be 粉 (ko, “powder”) plus an unclear suffix な (-na), first cited to 1683.

sources.quote: Appears to be 粉 (ko, “powder”, see above) + な (-na, suffixing element, meaning unclear).
First cited to 1683.

headline: Hā is onomatopoeic.

sources.quote: Onomatopoeic.

headline: Rōjin is compared with Proto-Ryukyuan *oe-pito, which uses native elements.

sources.quote: Compare Proto-Ryukyuan *oe-pito, using native elements.

headline: Nakayubi is 中 (naka, chū, “middle”) plus 指 (yubi, shi, “finger”).

sources.quote: 中 (naka, chū, “middle”) + 指 (yubi, shi, “finger”)

sources.quote: From English mistake or miss.
From English Miss.

headline: Hyōshiki is Middle Chinese 標識.

sources.quote: Middle Chinese 標識

headline: Ikenai is the negative of 行ける (ikeru), the potential form of 行く (iku).

sources.quote: Negative form of 行ける (ikeru), the potential form of 行く (iku).

headline: Ishi was coined by Nishi Amane as a translation of English will, and became established through the Tetsugaku Jii of Inoue Tetsujirō.

sources.quote: Coined by Japanese philosopher and politician Nishi Amane as a translation of English will, and became established by being included in the 哲学字彙 (Tetsugaku Jii, “Dictionary of Philosophy”) by Inoue Tetsujirō.

headline: Betsu ni is 別 (betsu, “separate”) plus に (ni): literally separately, used idiomatically to mean especially; compare Korean 별로 (byeollo).

sources.quote: 別 (betsu, “separate”) + に (ni, particle), literally separately, used idiomatically to mean something closer to especially. Compare Korean 별로 (byeollo).

sources.quote: 羊(よう) (yō, “sheep”) + 毛(もう) (mō, “hair”)

headline: Keredo is a clipping of けれども (keredomo, “although, but”), first attested in 1711.

sources.quote: Clipping of けれども (keredomo, “although, but”).
First attested in 1711.

headline: Saru's ultimate derivation is possibly borrowed from Ainu サロ (saro, “monkey”).

sources.quote: From Old Japanese. Appears in the Man'yōshū, completed some time after 759 CE.
Ultimate derivation possibly borrowed from Ainu サロ (saro, “monkey”, from サㇻ (sar, “a tail”) + オ (o, “to bear, to wear, to carry”)).
The kanji is from Chinese 猿 (yuán, “ape”). Compare Japanese 猪 (inoshishi, “boar”) from Chinese 猪 (zhū, “pig”) and Japanese 豚 (buta, “pig”) from Chinese 豚 (tún, “suckling pig”).

meaning: to rise; to grow; to mount (v.i.)
headline: Takamaru is 高 (taka, root of 高い, “high, tall”) plus -maru, developed from Classical Japanese 高む.

sources.quote: 高(たか) (taka, root of 高(たか)い (takai, “high, tall”)) + まる (-maru, “to become (an adjective), -en”), developed from Classical Japanese 高む.
